newsitem.title: GERMANY: French election result raises EMU doubts.
newsitem.headline: French election result raises EMU doubts.

text.p: Germany insisted on Monday that the sweeping election victory in France of the Socialist-led left would mean continued French support for Europe's planned single currency, but other countries were more cautious.

Some EU foreign ministers, meeting in Luxembourg, expressed reserve on the prospects for economic and monetary union (EMU) after Sunday's election, originally called by President Jacques Chirac to give new impetus to French efforts to qualify.

"I don't know, it depends who will be foreign minister," Dutch Foreign Minister Hans Van Mierlo said of the election result's possible effect on EMU's timetable. The Netherlands currently holds the rotating EU presidency.
European Commission president Jacques Santer, speaking in Brussels, stressed, however, that plans for EMU to start in 1999 were still on track.

Asked by reporters if the French election result could harm the credibility of the planned single currency and its timetable, Santer replied: "No, the timetable is in the treaty...that's an agreement reached at Maastricht and we have to stick to the commitments of the treaty."
Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi, speaking at a meeting near Bologna, said he believed Europe had been strengthened by the French left's win.

"I am thinking of a Europe where we return to the roots of the great continental European tradition, where the social state is transformed but cannot be swept away," said Prodi, whose centre-left government has been in power for one year in Italy.

British Prime Minister Tony Blair, whose Labour Party routed Conservatives in elections last month, congratulated French Socialist leader Lionel Jospin but would not be drawn on Jospin's comment that the British and French left-wing victories would "raise a magnificent hope in Europe."

A spokeswoman for Blair, who has promised a referendum before any British entry into EMU, said the prime minister telephoned Jospin on Sunday night and would be seeing conservative President Jacques Chirac on June 11.

Germany's Christian Democrat (CDU) Chancellor Helmut Kohl held a lengthy telephone conversation with Chirac on Monday. His foreign minister, Klaus Kinkel, said he was convinced of Paris's continued support for EMU.

Kinkel told reporters before a meeting of Free Democrat (FDP) party executives he was sure the planned euro currency would be launched on time and that countries participating would fulfil the criteria precisely.

"Germany and France remain for me the most important partners. We want to go further in Europe. The euro can be launched under strict adherence to the criteria and the planned timetable," Kinkel said.
In contrast, German newspapers voiced concern about the future of Europe's integration drive, and especially its planned common currency.

"Of the 15 European Union members, 12 are governed by or with the left, which does not want any more austerity for the euro in view of the social problems involved. For Bonn, it will be more difficult to push through 'pure Maastricht'," said the Frankfurter Rundschau.

Germany's left-wing opposition chief Oskar Lafontaine, whose Social Democrats will try to unseat Kohl in elections next year, hailed the French election result as a "a great success for France and for Europe."
Spanish Foreign Minister Abel Matutes said he did not expect the left-wing victory in France to have a significant effect on efforts to forge a more united Europe.
"I don't suppose there will be any change in the big decisions on the construction of Europe," Matutes told reporters in Luxembourg.
The United States congratulated France's Socialist Party and its allies on their election victory, with government officials and academic experts predicting little change in U.S.-French relations.
Portugal's Socialist Prime Minister Antonio Guterres welcomed the French election result, saying it would open the door to greater consensus on social issues.
"(I am) extremely pleased about the Socialist Party's great victory. It was a prize which Lionel Jospin deserved because of his coherence," Guterres told journalists.
"I am certain that this result will lead to greater consensus on employment and other social issues," he said.
